unit.title: Interpret and carry out electrical design

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which order of work is right when designing an installation?
options: Choose the cables, then find the loads, then pick a supply
Draw the layout, price it, then ask what the client needs
Find loads and supply, size the circuits, then check and record
Pick breakers to fill the board, then fit the loads to them

questions.stem: What does a single-line (one-line) diagram of an installation show?
options: The supply, boards, sub-mains and protective devices as simple lines
The exact route that each cable takes through the walls and ceilings
The terminal numbers and wire colours inside each control panel
The furniture layout for each room, drawn on the architect's plan

questions.stem: An electrician on site needs to know exactly where to fix each outlet in an office. Which drawing should he work from?
options: The single-line diagram of the boards
The schematic of the lighting controls
The schedule of circuits for the board
The dimensioned layout drawing of the floor

questions.stem: Why might a designer fit a 300 mA RCD at the origin of a farm building, as well as 30 mA RCDs on its outlet circuits?
options: The 300 mA device trips faster than the 30 mA devices below it
The 300 mA device lets the outlets run at a higher voltage
The 300 mA guards against fire from leakage; the 30 mA guard people
The 300 mA device means the outlets need no earth conductor

questions.stem: A cable's table rating is 40 A. The design data gives a factor of 0.94 for air temperature and 0.7 for grouping. What is its corrected rating?
In design, what does discrimination (selectivity) between protective devices mean?
options: Every device in the building trips together on any fault
Only the device nearest the fault trips, so others stay on
The main switch trips first, so the whole building is safe
Each device is a different make, so faults are easy to trace

questions.stem: A 63 A sub-main breaker feeds a board with 32 A outgoing breakers. How is discrimination between them usually confirmed at the design stage?
options: By choosing breakers that all have the same rating
By assuming a larger breaker always discriminates
By short-circuiting the circuit live on site to see
By checking the makers' tables or time-current curves

questions.stem: Design data gives a prospective fault current of 12 kA at a new board. Which breaking capacity should its breakers have?
options: 6 kA
10 kA
15 kA
Any, as breakers trip on any fault

questions.stem: In the lumen method, N = (E × A) ÷ (F × UF × MF). Which change means more fittings are needed?
options: A higher lux level is required
The utilisation factor goes up
Lamps with more lumens are used
The room is made smaller

questions.stem: In the lumen method, why is a maintenance factor used?
options: To allow for the cost of new lamps each year
To allow for dirt and the fall in light output over time
To allow for the hours the lights are off at night
To allow for the volt drop along the lighting circuit

questions.stem: On a 110/220 V split-phase board, line 1 carries 40 A and line 2 carries 25 A of 110 V resistive loads. What current flows in the shared neutral?
options: 0 A

questions.stem: Why does the designer share the 110 V circuits evenly between the two lines of a split-phase board?
options: So each line can use a smaller earth conductor than usual
So the meter records less energy than the building uses
So the 220 V loads can be fed from one line and neutral
So the neutral current and the load on each line stay low

questions.stem: A 220 V load draws 50 A at a power factor of 0.9. What is its real power?
options: 9.9 kW

questions.stem: A 50 kW load draws 37.5 kVAR at a power factor of 0.8. At 0.95 it would draw about 16.4 kVAR. About what size of capacitor bank is needed?
options: 16.4 kVAR
21.1 kVAR
37.5 kVAR
53.9 kVAR

questions.stem: A building's maximum demand is 120 kW at a power factor of 0.9. Transformers come in 100, 150 and 200 kVA. Before allowing for growth, which is the smallest that will do?
options: 100 kVA
120 kVA
150 kVA
200 kVA

questions.stem: Why must a standby generator be sized for more than the running load when large motors are connected to it?
options: Motors make a generator run above its rated 50 Hz
Motors draw less current from a generator than from mains
Motors start only when the generator's tank is quite full
Motor starting current can dip the voltage and stall the set

questions.stem: In a TN-C-S system, where does the installation's earth connection come from?
options: Only from the installation's own earth rod
From the supplier's combined neutral and earth conductor
From the water pipes of the house next door
From the metal roof sheets of the building

questions.stem: Why is RCD protection usually designed in for circuits in a TT system?
options: The electrode's resistance is often too high for a breaker to trip fast
A TT system has no neutral conductor anywhere in the whole installation
RCDs stop the meter from turning when the building has no load
Ordinary breakers are not allowed in a TT system at any point

questions.stem: A design puts one surge protective device at the main board and another at a sub-board feeding computers. Why both?
options: The second one takes every surge, so the first lasts longer
One works for the day supply and one for the night supply
The main one takes the big surge; the local one limits the rest
Two are needed so that the RCDs do not trip during a storm

questions.stem: The specification allows 5% total volt drop on a 220 V supply. The sub-main drops 4.4 V. How much may the final circuit drop?
Cable data gives 7.3 mV/A/m. A 220 V circuit carries 25 A over 30 m, and the specification allows 3%. Is the cable acceptable?
options: Yes: the drop is about 5.5 V, under the 6.6 V allowed
No: the drop is about 7.3 V, over the 6.6 V allowed
No: the drop is about 55 V, far over the limit
Yes: the drop is about 2.2 V, well under the limit

questions.stem: Why is a motor circuit's breaker often rated above the motor's full-load current, with a separate overload relay?
options: A breaker set at full-load current would make the motor run too fast
The breaker rides through starting; the overload protects the motor
The overload relay protects the cable against short circuits only
The breaker is chosen by the motor's weight and not its current

questions.stem: A drawing note says 'all heights to finished floor level (FFL) unless noted'. An outlet is marked 450. Where is it fixed?
options: 450 mm above the bare concrete slab
450 mm down from the finished ceiling
450 mm above the finished floor
450 mm from the nearest door frame

questions.stem: A board schedule shows circuit 7 as '20 A, 2.5 mm², 30 mA RCBO, kitchen outlets'. What does '30 mA' tell the installer?
options: The circuit's design current is 30 mA
The cable is rated to carry 30 mA
The device trips at 30 A of overload
The device trips on 30 mA of earth leakage

questions.stem: On site, a beam blocks the cable route on the design, and the new route is 15 m longer. What should the supervisor do?
options: Fit the longer route and say nothing, as the cable is the same
Check volt drop and loop impedance with the designer; record it
Use a smaller cable on the new route to make up the extra cost
Leave the circuit out until the rest of the building is finished

questions.stem: An office floor has many LED drivers and computers on a three-phase supply. Why might the designer make the neutral larger?
options: Harmonic currents from these loads add up in the neutral
LED drivers always need a neutral twice the line size
Computers run on DC, so they need a bigger neutral
A larger neutral makes the LED lights shine brighter

questions.stem: A cable must run underground from a house to a pump at the gate. Which cable choice suits best?
options: Flat twin-and-earth PVC cable laid with no protection
A flexible cord of the kind used for appliances
Armoured cable, or cable in a duct, as specified
Bare copper conductors laid straight in the soil

questions.stem: Where should a designer place emergency luminaires along an escape route?
options: Only in the main office, over the manager's desk
Only outside the building, over the car park
Only in the toilets, where people may be alone
At exits, changes of direction, stairs and fire points

questions.stem: Which circuit would a designer most likely specify in fire-resistant cable?
options: The fire alarm and the fire pump supply
A bedroom outlet circuit in a private house
The garden lighting by the car park
A water heater circuit in a bathroom

questions.stem: Before a design is issued, why does a second engineer check it?
options: To share the design fee with another engineer
To catch errors in sums, choices and drawings
To change the client's brief to suit the contractor
To approve it in place of the government inspector

questions.stem: The specification says all outlet circuits must have RCD protection of 30 mA or less. A drawing shows an outlet circuit with a plain breaker. What is right?
options: Follow the drawing, as drawings always overrule the specification
Fit a 100 mA RCD as a middle choice between the two documents
Raise a query with the designer and follow the written answer
Leave the circuit without protection until handover is close

questions.stem: A design has 10 outlet circuits of 20 A. The design data says: take the first circuit at 100% and the rest at 40%. What demand is used?
Why is a 2-pole breaker used for a 220 V circuit on a split-phase board?
options: Both lines are live, so both are switched and protected together
A 2-pole breaker trips at half the current that a 1-pole one needs
The neutral must be switched by the second pole of the breaker
It lets the circuit run at 110 V and at 220 V at the same time

questions.stem: Why must a protective conductor be large enough to carry the fault current until the protective device opens?
options: So it stays cool in everyday use
So it is not damaged and stays intact
So it can be used as a spare neutral
So the RCD does not trip on normal load

questions.stem: Why might a designer specify XLPE-insulated cable rather than PVC for circuits in a hot plant room?
options: XLPE cable is always cheaper to buy than PVC cable
XLPE cable needs no protective conductor at all
XLPE can run at a higher conductor temperature
XLPE cable can be laid with no supports or clips

questions.stem: In a large open office, why does the designer put the row of lights nearest the windows on its own switch or sensor?
options: Lights by the windows need a higher voltage than the rest
Those lights must stay on all night for the security guard
It helps the cleaners find the windows in the evening
They can be dimmed or turned off when daylight is enough

questions.stem: Which set of documents should a complete design package include?
options: Drawings, single-line diagram, schedules, calculations, specification
Drawings, timesheets, wage slips and the site diary for the job
The client's bank details and the contractor's insurance cover papers
Product brochures only, with the prices marked on each page

questions.stem: An A/C unit's nameplate reads '220 V, MCA 15 A, MOP 25 A'. What does MOP tell the designer?
options: The smallest cable size the maker will allow
The largest protective device the maker allows
The running current of the unit's compressor
The output power of the fan motor in horsepower

questions.stem: A split-phase board feeds a 220 V, 22 A water heater, and 10 A of 110 V lights on line 1 only. What current flows in line 1?
Why does a designer place a sub-board in the far wing of a long hotel, instead of running every circuit from the main board?
options: A sub-board lets the far wing run at its own frequency
Sub-boards remove the need for protective conductors
Long circuits are cheaper but need a building permit
Shorter final circuits keep volt drop and Zs down

questions.stem: A fuel station design has pumps inside a hazardous area. What must the design specify for electrical equipment in that zone?
options: Equipment certified for that zone, as the specification says
Ordinary outlets, fixed higher up the wall than usual
Plastic boxes painted bright red so they are easily seen
Extra lighting so that the drivers can see the pumps clearly at night

questions.stem: A schematic shows a contactor coil with a stop button in series, and a start button with a contact of the same contactor in parallel across it. What does that contact do?
options: It trips the motor out when it is overloaded
It keeps the coil on after the start button is let go
It reverses the direction the motor turns
It stops the motor when the guard door opens

questions.stem: A design uses 21 LED fittings of 36 W each on one 110 V circuit. About what current will the circuit draw?
A trainee asks why he cannot swap the 10 mm² sub-main on the design for the 6 mm² cable left in the van. What is the best reply?
options: He can, as long as he also fits a smaller breaker
He can, because the 6 mm² cable is newer stock
He can, if the real run is shorter than shown
No: it was sized for load, volt drop and faults

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a factor in choosing a cable's size?
options: The design current of the circuit
The colour of the outer sheath
The air temperature along the route
The volt drop that is allowed

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the term for the amount of light falling on a surface, measured in lux?
Which device in a motor starter protects the motor against too much current for too long, and is set to the full-load current?
The design data for a pump room gives 40 kW of real power and 50 kVA of apparent power. What power factor is that?
What is the current a circuit is expected to carry in normal use called, written Ib on a schedule? (two words)
Does kVAR measure real power, apparent power or reactive power?
A 6 m by 5 m room needs 300 lux. Each fitting gives 3 000 lm, the utilisation factor is 0.5 and the maintenance factor is 0.8. How many fittings are needed (whole number)?
What is the largest current that would flow in a short circuit at a point called, used to choose breaking capacity? (words or letters)
In the lumen method formula, what do the letters UF stand for?
What is the drawing called that shows how control devices, coils and contacts are connected, but not where they are fixed?
On a design schedule, which symbol stands for the rated current of the protective device? (letters)
Which item of equipment is added to an installation to improve its power factor by supplying reactive power?
On a layout drawn to 1:50, the run from the board to the pump isolator is 120 mm long on paper. What is the real length, in metres?
What is the term for a protective device's ability to safely break the largest fault current it may see, given in kA? (two words)
What is the current a motor takes at its rated output, shown on its nameplate, called? (words or letters)
A long run of PVC conduit on a sunny roof needs a fitting that lets it grow and shrink with heat. What is that fitting called?

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to design the electrical installation for a small office in Half Way Tree, from the client's brief to the issued design.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from the agreed brief and the architect's drawings, and visit the site to confirm the supply. I would list every load and work out the maximum demand using the diversity in the design data, and agree the supply with the power company. Next I would lay out the lights, outlets, data points and equipment on the floor plan, using the lumen method for the lighting. I would group the points into circuits and share them evenly between the two lines of the split-phase board. For each circuit I would find the design current, choose the protective device, and size the cable using the correction factors, then check the volt drop and the earth fault loop impedance. I would check the fault level for breaking capacity and the discrimination between devices. I would draw the single-line diagram and the board schedules, write the specification, have the design checked by another engineer, and then issue it with a revision letter.
markingPoints: Starts from the brief and drawings and confirms the supply
Works out loads and maximum demand, and lays out the points
Groups circuits and balances them across the lines
Sizes devices and cables with correction factors, and checks volt drop, loop impedance, fault level and discrimination
Produces drawings, schedules and specification, has the design checked, and issues it

essays.stem: A 220 V sub-main has a design current of 48 A and is 40 m long. Breakers come in 50 A and 63 A. Cable A has a table rating of 57 A and 4.4 mV/A/m; cable B has 76 A and 2.8 mV/A/m. The correction factor is 0.87, and the specification allows 3% volt drop on the sub-main. Choose the breaker and the cable, and show your working.
essays.modelAnswer: The breaker must be at least the design current, so the 50 A breaker is chosen, since 50 A is not less than 48 A. The cable's corrected rating must be at least the breaker rating. Cable A: 57 × 0.87 = 49.6 A, which is less than 50 A, so cable A fails. Cable B: 76 × 0.87 = 66.1 A, which is more than 50 A, so it passes on current. Next the volt drop. The limit is 3% of 220 V = 6.6 V. For cable B, volt drop = 2.8 × 48 × 40 ÷ 1000 = 5.38 V, which is under 6.6 V, so it passes. (Cable A would drop 4.4 × 48 × 40 ÷ 1000 = 8.45 V, so it would fail on volt drop too.) The choice is a 50 A breaker with cable B. I would still check that the breaker's breaking capacity suits the fault level at the board, that it discriminates with the device upstream, and that the earth fault loop impedance is low enough.
markingPoints: Chooses the 50 A breaker because it is not below 48 A
Corrects cable ratings: A = 49.6 A (fails), B = 66.1 A (passes)
Works out the 6.6 V limit and the 5.38 V drop for cable B
Selects the 50 A breaker with cable B
Mentions the further checks: fault level, discrimination and loop impedance

essays.stem: Explain the lumen method of lighting design, and use it for a classroom 12 m by 6 m that needs 400 lux. Each fitting gives 3 600 lm, the utilisation factor is 0.55 and the maintenance factor is 0.8.
essays.modelAnswer: The lumen method works out how many fittings are needed to give an average light level on the working plane. The formula is N = (E × A) ÷ (F × UF × MF). E is the lux needed, A is the floor area, F is the lumens from one fitting, UF is the utilisation factor (the share of the light that reaches the working plane, which depends on the room shape and the surface colours), and MF is the maintenance factor (allowing for dirt and the fall in light output over time). Here the area is 12 × 6 = 72 m². The light needed is 400 × 72 = 28 800 lm. Each fitting gives 3 600 × 0.55 × 0.8 = 1 584 lm usable. So N = 28 800 ÷ 1 584 = 18.2, which rounds up to 19 fittings. For an even layout I would use 20 fittings, in four rows of five, and check the spacing against the maker's spacing-to-height ratio.
markingPoints: States the formula and explains each term
Explains utilisation factor and maintenance factor
Works out the area (72 m²) and lumens needed (28 800 lm)
Works out N = 18.2 and rounds up to 19
Arranges an even layout (for example 20) and checks spacing

essays.stem: Explain what discrimination between protective devices is, why it matters in a hotel, and how you would achieve it between the main switch, a sub-main breaker and the final-circuit breakers.
essays.modelAnswer: Discrimination, or selectivity, means that when a fault happens, only the protective device closest to the fault opens, and the devices upstream stay closed. In a hotel this matters because a fault on one guest room's outlet circuit should not black out a whole floor or the kitchen. To achieve it, I would make each upstream device larger and slower than the ones below it. I would check the makers' time-current curves to see that the curves do not cross over the range of fault currents expected, or use the makers' discrimination tables, which show the fault current up to which two devices discriminate. Rough rules, such as one size bigger, are not enough at high fault currents. For RCDs, I would use a time-delayed type upstream with 30 mA devices on the final circuits. I would record the chosen devices and settings in the design, so they are not changed on site.
markingPoints: Defines discrimination: only the nearest device opens
Explains why it matters for a hotel (keeps other areas on)
Upstream devices larger and slower than downstream
Uses makers' curves or discrimination tables, not rules of thumb
Uses time-delayed RCDs upstream, and records the choices

essays.stem: A factory takes 80 kW at a power factor of 0.75. Explain what power factor is, why a low power factor is a problem, and work out the size of capacitor bank needed to raise it to 0.95.
essays.modelAnswer: Power factor is the ratio of real power, in kW, to apparent power, in kVA. Motors and some lighting draw reactive power as well as real power, so the current is higher than the useful power needs. A low power factor means larger currents, so cables, switchgear and transformers must be bigger, losses are higher, and the power company may charge for it. At 0.75, the apparent power is 80 ÷ 0.75 = 106.7 kVA. The reactive power is the square root of (106.7² − 80²) = about 70.5 kVAR. At 0.95, the apparent power is 80 ÷ 0.95 = 84.2 kVA, and the reactive power is the square root of (84.2² − 80²) = about 26.3 kVAR. So the capacitor bank must supply about 70.5 − 26.3 = 44 kVAR. I would choose the next standard size, consider automatic stepped control so the factory is not over-corrected at light load, and make sure the bank has discharge resistors.
markingPoints: Defines power factor as kW ÷ kVA
Explains the effects of a low power factor (current, size, losses, charges)
Works out 106.7 kVA and about 70.5 kVAR at 0.75
Works out 84.2 kVA and about 26.3 kVAR at 0.95
Finds about 44 kVAR and mentions standard size, stepped control or discharge

essays.stem: Explain how you would share the circuits of a house between the two lines of a 110/220 V split-phase board, and why. Use an example with figures.
essays.modelAnswer: A split-phase board has two lines, each 110 V to neutral, with 220 V between them. The 220 V loads, such as the A/C units, the stove and the water heater, are on 2-pole breakers and draw the same current from both lines, so they do not upset the balance. The 110 V circuits, such as lights and outlets, each use one line and the neutral. With resistive loads, the neutral carries the difference between the two lines' 110 V currents. I would list each 110 V circuit with its expected current and place them in turn on line 1 and line 2 so the totals are about equal. For example, if line 1 carries 45 A and line 2 carries 30 A of 110 V load, the neutral carries about 15 A. Moving a 7 A circuit from line 1 to line 2 gives 38 A and 37 A, and only about 1 A in the neutral. Balancing keeps line currents down, lowers volt drop and losses, and lets the main switch carry the most useful load.
markingPoints: Describes the split-phase supply (two lines, 110 V and 220 V)
220 V loads on 2-pole breakers draw from both lines equally
Neutral carries the difference of the 110 V line currents
Gives a correct worked example of balancing
Explains the benefits (lower currents, volt drop, losses)

essays.stem: Explain how you would design the standby supply for a small hotel: choosing the essential loads, sizing the generator and arranging the changeover.
essays.modelAnswer: With the client I would choose the essential loads: for example the emergency and corridor lighting, the kitchen fridges and freezers, the water pumps, the front desk and the computer server, and some A/C. I would list each with its kW, power factor and starting current. I would add up the running load with the diversity in the design data, then check the largest motor starting, because a large pump or compressor starting can dip the voltage and stall the set. I would size the generator in kVA with a margin for growth, or plan to start large motors one at a time or with soft starters. The essential circuits would go on their own board, fed through an automatic transfer switch that is interlocked so the generator can never feed back into the power company's lines. I would size the cables for both supplies, check the protection still works when fed from the generator, and plan the fuel, exhaust and ventilation.
markingPoints: Chooses the essential loads with the client
Lists kW, power factor and starting currents and applies diversity
Sizes the generator in kVA, allowing for motor starting and growth
Uses an essential board and an interlocked transfer switch to stop back-feed
Checks cables and protection on generator supply, and plans fuel and ventilation

essays.stem: You are the supervisor carrying out someone else's design on a new shop fit-out. Explain how you would interpret the design documents and deal with problems found on site.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check that I have the latest revision of every drawing, schedule and the specification, and read them together: the layout drawings for positions, the single-line diagram and board schedules for devices and cables, and the specification for materials and workmanship. I would list anything unclear or in conflict, for example a drawing that shows a plain breaker where the specification asks for RCD protection. I would not guess. I would send a written query, often called a request for information, to the designer, and work to the written answer. If a site problem forces a change, such as a beam in the way of a cable route, I would ask the designer to check its effect on volt drop, loop impedance and cable rating before work goes ahead. I would brief the team, mark every agreed change on a site copy of the drawings, and use those marks to produce the as-built drawings at the end.
markingPoints: Checks the latest revisions and reads drawings, schedules and specification together
Lists unclear or conflicting items
Raises written queries (RFIs) and works to the written answer
Has the designer check the effect of any site change
Briefs the team and records changes for the as-built drawings

essays.stem: Explain how you would design the earthing, bonding and surge protection for a new house on a hillside in St Ann, where lightning is common.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would find out how the power company earths its supply, because that decides the earthing system the design uses and whether the installation's own electrode is the main earth path or a backup. I would plan a main earthing terminal at the board, with an earthing conductor to one or more earth rods. On rocky ground a low resistance may be hard to get, so I may need more rods, deeper rods or a different electrode as the specification allows, and I would set a target value to be tested. I would bond the incoming metal water pipe and any other metal services to the main earthing terminal. Where the electrode resistance is high, I would make sure RCDs give fast disconnection. For lightning, I would put a surge protective device at the main board and another near sensitive equipment such as the TV and computer, with short, straight connections to earth, and choose types and ratings that coordinate, as the makers say.
markingPoints: Finds the supply's earthing arrangement first
Plans the main earthing terminal, earthing conductor and electrode(s) with a target value
Allows for rocky ground with extra or deeper electrodes
Bonds incoming metal services and uses RCDs where needed
Coordinated SPDs at the board and near equipment, with short earth connections

essays.stem: Explain how an electrical design should be checked and documented before it is issued for construction, and why each step matters.
essays.modelAnswer: The designer first checks their own work against the brief and the specification: that every room has the points agreed, and that the loads and maximum demand are right. Each circuit's calculation is checked: design current, device rating, corrected cable rating, volt drop, loop impedance, fault level and discrimination. A second, competent engineer then checks the design independently, because it is easy to miss your own mistakes. The design package is put together: layout drawings, the single-line diagram, board schedules, calculations and the specification, all with the same revision letter and date. Any assumptions, such as cable routes or demand factors, are written down so they can be checked later. The design is signed by the person responsible, and a register of drawings shows what has been issued. These steps matter because errors found on paper are cheap to fix, while errors found after installation cost money, delay the job, and can make the installation unsafe.
markingPoints: Checks the design against the brief and specification
Checks each circuit's calculations
Independent check by a second competent engineer
Complete, consistent package with revisions, assumptions and signatures
Explains that errors on paper are cheaper and safer to fix

practical1.title: Design the installation for a small office from a brief
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a brief and a floor plan for a small two-room office with a toilet and a kitchenette, fed from a 110/220 V split-phase supply. The assessor also gives cable tables, correction factors, a volt-drop limit, lumen data for a light fitting, and a list of equipment ratings. As a group, give each member a role (design lead, lighting designer, circuit designer, calculations checker, and drawings and schedules lead) and swap so that everyone works at least one calculation. Produce: a lighting design for each room using the lumen method; a layout drawing showing lights, switches, outlets and the board; a load list with the maximum demand; a board schedule with the circuits shared between the two lines and the neutral current worked out; the device and cable choice for each circuit, with the correction factors and volt drop checked; and a single-line diagram. A different member checks each calculation and signs it. Finally, present the design to the assessor, who plays the client.
materials: Brief and floor plan of a small office (from the assessor)
Cable tables, correction factors, volt-drop limit and lumen data (assessor's data)
A3 paper, scale rulers, templates for electrical symbols, pencils
Blank board schedule and calculation sheets
photos: The lighting calculation for each room
The layout drawing with symbols and a key
The load list and maximum demand
The board schedule with the line balance and neutral current
The cable and device calculations, signed by the checker
The single-line diagram and the presentation to the client
checklist: Worked a lumen method calculation correctly
Drew symbols and positions clearly and to scale
Balanced the 110 V circuits between the two lines
Chose devices and cables correctly using the data, with volt drop checked
Checked another member's calculation and found any error
Explained the design clearly to the client
Kept all sheets neat, titled, dated and signed
safety: This is a desk task: no equipment is opened or energised
The design must include RCD protection and earthing as the specification requires
Use the data the assessor gives; do not guess figures

practical2.title: Interpret a design and build it on a training bay
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a design package for a small installation on a training bay that is NOT connected to any supply: a layout drawing, a single-line diagram, a board schedule and a short specification. One planted discrepancy between the documents is included. As a group, give each member a role (supervisor, two installers, materials and labelling lead, and records lead) and swap so that everyone installs and terminates. Isolate and lock off the bay's supply point with every member's padlock and a tag, and prove dead with a tester checked before and after use. Read the documents, list the materials from the schedule, and find the discrepancy: write a request for information to the assessor (the designer) and work to the written answer. Mark out and install the board, containment and circuits as designed: correct devices and cable sizes, circuits on the lines the schedule shows, labels and the circuit chart. Carry out dead tests (continuity and insulation resistance) and record them. Mark up a drawing as built.
materials: Training bay not connected to any supply, with a lockable supply point
Design package with one planted discrepancy (from the assessor)
Split-phase training board, breakers including 2-pole and RCD types
Cable, conduit or trunking and accessories as the schedule lists
Lock-off kit with a multi-lock hasp, one padlock per member, and tags
Two-pole voltage tester and proving unit
Hand tools, spirit level, measuring tape and labelling materials
Blank RFI form, test sheet and a spare copy of the drawing for marking up
photos: The supply point locked off with every member's padlock and a tag
The tester checked on the proving unit before and after proving dead
The written RFI and the designer's answer
The board with devices matching the schedule, and its circuit chart
The finished circuits and containment on the bay
The completed test sheet and the marked-up as-built drawing
checklist: Isolated, locked off and proved dead correctly, with the tester checked before and after
Read the documents correctly and found the discrepancy
Wrote a clear RFI and followed the written answer
Installed devices and cables exactly as the design and schedule state
Fitted correct labels and completed the circuit chart
Carried out and recorded dead tests correctly
Marked up the as-built drawing accurately and left the bay tidy
safety: The bay stays dead and locked off throughout; only the instructor ever energises anything
Every member fits their own padlock before any work starts
Warn others before each insulation test and let the circuit discharge before touching it
Wear eye protection when drilling or cutting, and keep the work area clear
